rv.q: Proffering the catharsis of honesty, the recognition of absurdity and the comfort of fellow feeling, the show traces the life cycle of motherhood, and what mothers lose and gain along the way.
For Ogawa, these are ways to bring effervescence and intimacy to the contemplation of insoluble, heavy things.
A project of this kind requires a spiky anarchic insouciance that neither the writing nor the performances consistently achieve.
The more bonkers the sketch, the more relatable Meat Suit becomes.
At once absurdly funny, divinely bizarre, and absurdly poignant, Meat Show finds a new and exciting way to express the trials, tribulations, and thrills of having children.
A show that probably gives voice to the hidden anguish of some in the audience, Meat Suit is just as likely to be an ordeal for others.
In Meat Suit, the truth is readily apparent – motherhood can indeed be a shitshow – but the execution is neither all that funny or entertaining.
As it is, the high jinks overwhelm the ideas they’re meant to illuminate.
This circus is lively—but the tricks never quite astonish.

cn.t: Critics are divided on Ogawa's audacious, grotesque exploration of motherhood's darker side—some praise its bold satire and playful horror, while others find it exhaustingly rambling and one-note in its relentless negativity.

vr.q: My overall impression of the piece, though, was definitely a mixed bag.
